planting.note: Break off a rooted offset or short stem section, let the cut end callus for a couple of days, then set it shallowly into a very gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright light.

directions: Huernia hystrix forms clumping mats of four-angled stems entirely covered in soft, fleshy, bristle-tipped tubercles, giving the plant a quilled, porcupine-like texture that is unusual even among the bristly Huernia clan. Its star-shaped flowers are pale cream to yellow with dark maroon mottling and fine marginal hairs along each pointed lobe, releasing a faint carrion odor that draws fly pollinators. Grow in bright light with a little midday shade in the hottest climates, in an especially fast-draining mineral mix, since the congested stem clusters rot quickly if kept damp. Water only once the mix is fully dry and reduce watering sharply through winter dormancy.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in a very lean, mineral, fast-draining mix in full sun, and withhold water entirely during the annual split when the old leaf pair shrivels and a new pair emerges from within.

directions: Lithops hookeri produces paired, fused, stone-mimicking leaves with reddish-brown to ochre top faces marked by darker branching fissures and raised islands that break up the outline against gravel, one of the larger-bodied and more vigorously clumping species in the genus. Bright yellow daisy-like flowers emerge from the fissure between the leaves in late summer to fall, usually opening only in strong sunlight. It needs the brightest light available for compact growth and strong surface patterning, along with a gritty, low-organic mix that drains almost instantly. Water sparingly during active growth and stop completely while the plant is resting or splitting to avoid rotting the developing new pair.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in a very lean, mineral, fast-draining mix in full sun, and withhold water entirely during the annual split when the old leaf pair shrivels and a new pair emerges from within.

directions: Lithops marmorata carries pale grey to near-white top faces threaded with dark green, branching veins that resemble the veining of polished marble, a cooler and starker coloration than the reddish or ochre tones typical of many other Lithops species. Clean white daisy-like flowers appear in the fall from the central fissure and usually open only in bright afternoon sun. This species is especially sensitive to overwatering because of its pale, thin-skinned leaves, so plant it in an ultra-porous mineral mix and set it in full sun for the tightest, most compact body form. Keep it bone dry during the winter split and resume light watering only once the new leaf pair has fully hardened off.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in a very lean, mineral, fast-draining mix in full sun, and withhold water entirely during the annual split when the old leaf pair shrivels and a new pair emerges from within.

directions: Lithops otzeniana forms rounded, grey-green to warm brown bodies whose flat or slightly domed top faces are traced with a network of darker reddish channels and scattered translucent dots that function as light-admitting windows, camouflaging the plant among the quartzite gravel of its native habitat. Golden yellow flowers open from the central fissure in late summer and early fall, typically unfurling only under strong direct sun. It clumps more readily than many living stones, slowly forming small multi-headed groups when given generous light and a strictly mineral, fast-draining substrate. Keep completely dry through the winter resting period so the new leaf pair can absorb the old pair without rot setting in.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant in a lean, mineral, fast-draining mix in full sun and let the surface dry out completely between waterings to keep the thick paired leaves from splitting or rotting.

directions: Pleiospilos bolusii forms one or two pairs of thick, almost hemispherical grey-green leaves flecked with fine darker dots, closely resembling a cluster of weathered granite pebbles and growing noticeably larger and more angular per pair than the related, more rounded Pleiospilos nelii. Large, sweetly scented, coconut-tinged golden-yellow flowers open in late summer to fall, often nearly as wide as the plant body itself. Give it the brightest light possible year-round to keep growth compact and stone-like, since low light quickly causes the leaves to stretch and lose their camouflage form. Water only sparingly during active growth and withhold water almost entirely in the heat of summer and through winter dormancy to prevent rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets or root fresh leaf-pair cuttings in a gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Faucaria felina forms low clumps of fleshy, triangular, blue-green leaves edged with a handful of soft, elongated, backward-curving teeth along each margin, a coarser and more sparsely toothed jaw than the dense fine teeth of its close relative Faucaria tigrina. Large, glossy golden-yellow daisy-like flowers open in the afternoon during fall, closing again each evening for several weeks of bloom. Grow in full sun to light shade in a fast-draining, mineral succulent mix, watering moderately in the growing season and allowing the soil to dry fully between waterings. Reduce water sharply in winter, since the compact, shallow-rooted rosettes are prone to rot in cold, damp soil.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in a very lean, mineral, fast-draining mix in full sun, keeping the almost stemless bodies nearly dry through summer dormancy.

directions: Argyroderma testiculare forms paired, almost stemless, silvery grey-green bodies so rounded and fused that each pair resembles a single smooth button or pebble sitting flush with the soil surface, one of the more compact and classic forms in a genus known for extreme leaf fusion. Large magenta to deep purple flowers, often wider than the plant body itself, open in early to mid fall and are followed by a brief flush of new growth before summer dormancy sets in. Plant in a strictly mineral, fast-draining mix and give it full sun for the tightest, most stone-like form. Water only lightly during the cooler growing months and keep nearly bone dry through the hot summer rest period to prevent the fused bodies from splitting or rotting.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in full sun; raise the thickening base partly above the soil line in a shallow pot as the caudex develops to display its bonsai-like form.

directions: Trichodiadema densum develops a dense, low, shrubby crown of wiry stems set with tiny cylindrical leaves, each tip ringed by a crown of fine white bristles that catch the light and give the growing points a frosted, star-studded look. Over years of cultivation the base swells into a thick, gnarled, woody caudex that growers often expose above the soil to create a miniature tree-like specimen for bonsai-style display. Bright magenta daisy-like flowers appear repeatedly through the warm growing season on short stalks above the foliage. Grow in full sun with a strictly mineral, fast-draining mix, watering moderately when active and cutting back hard on water in winter to protect the caudex from rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; it roots readily along trailing stems to knit into a dense mat.

directions: Oscularia deltoides forms sprawling, woody-based mats of small, triangular, blue-grey leaves edged with fine reddish teeth along each keeled face, flushing pink to purple-tinted in strong sun and cool weather. In spring the entire mat can disappear beneath a dense flush of small, fragrant, bright magenta-pink daisy flowers that open on sunny days. It is a workhorse groundcover for slopes, rock gardens, and container spillers, tolerating poor, lean, fast-draining soil and reflected heat far better than richer garden loam. Water sparingly once established and shear lightly after the main bloom flush to keep the mat tight and encourage rebloom.

planting.note: Set the clustered leaves shallowly in a very lean, sandy mineral mix so only the flattened, translucent leaf tips sit at or just above the soil surface, in bright full sun.

directions: Frithia pulchra grows almost entirely buried in sandy soil, with only the blunt, flattened tips of its finger-like leaves showing above the surface; each tip carries a translucent window that lets light reach the leaf's interior tissue for photosynthesis while the rest of the plant stays hidden and protected underground. Slender pink to purple daisy-like flowers rise from the center of the cluster in spring and summer, opening in full sun. Because the plant naturally sits nearly flush with the soil, plant it shallowly in a very sandy, mineral mix rather than burying it as deeply as a typical succulent, and give it the brightest light available. It is slow to bulk up from seed and sensitive to overwatering, so let the mix dry out fully between waterings and reduce water further outside the growing season.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in a very porous, mineral succulent mix in full sun; as a winter grower it should be watered mainly from fall through spring and kept nearly dry through its summer dormancy.

directions: Aloinopsis schooneesii forms dense, spreading mats of small clustered rosettes, each made up of plump, dark blue-green leaves with finely textured surfaces and blunt, triangular tips that echo the look of scattered gravel. From a swollen, tuberous root, the plant sends up bronze-yellow daisy-like flowers with a darker central stripe on each petal, opening only in the late afternoon or early evening from late winter into spring. Unlike many mesembs that rest in winter, this species grows actively through the cooler months and goes dormant in summer heat, so watering should follow that reversed rhythm. Give it full sun and an extremely porous mineral mix, and withhold water almost entirely during its summer rest to prevent the low, congested mats from rotting.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in a sandy, mineral-rich, fast-draining mix in full sun; as a winter grower it takes regular light watering from fall through winter and should be kept dry through summer dormancy.

directions: Cheiridopsis purpurea forms small, clump-forming shrublets of paired, keeled, pale grey-green leaves joined at the base when young and separating as they mature, with older leaf pairs drying into papery, corky brown sheaths that wrap and protect each new growth point. Brilliant magenta flowers up to several inches across open around midday and close again by evening during the winter bloom season, standing out sharply against the muted grey foliage. Native to rocky sandstone crevices in the Richtersveld, it needs a sandy, mineral-rich, fast-draining mix and full sun to develop its best color and compact form. Water lightly through the cooler growing months, including an occasional fine misting, and withhold water almost entirely during summer dormancy.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in an extremely well-drained, loamy-mineral mix with some shelter from all-day baking sun, watering only occasionally year-round.

directions: Gibbaeum heathii forms small clumps of paired, thick, rounded leaf-bodies pressed tightly together with a distinct fissure between them, each pair covered in a fine downy texture and colored from soft green to whitish-green, giving the whole cluster a plump, pebble-like appearance. White, cream, or pale pink flowers emerge from between the leaf pairs from late winter into early spring, often nearly covering the small bodies when the clump is well established. Native to hot, rocky plains in South Africa's Little Karoo, it needs exceptionally sharp drainage along with some protection from the most intense midday sun, unlike more sun-hardy Lithops relatives. Water only sparingly throughout the year and let the mix dry completely between waterings to avoid rot in the closely packed bodies.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in sandy, rocky, extremely fast-draining soil in full sun with no fertilizer, keeping the mostly buried body nearly dry outside active growth.

directions: Dinteranthus vanzylii, a close relative of Lithops, forms a nearly fused pair of leaves with only a narrow fissure between them, sitting mostly below the soil surface so that just the top of the pair is visible, unlike other Dinteranthus species that sit fully exposed. Leaf color ranges from chalky white and grey to coppery brown, often with faint darker markings that help the small body blend into surrounding rock and gravel. Solitary flowers in bright yellow to orange, sometimes over an inch across, open from the central fissure in late summer to fall. Plant in sandy to rocky, extremely well-drained soil in full sun with no fertilizer, and water only sparingly during the growing season, keeping the plant essentially dry the rest of the year to prevent rot in its low, buried form.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Cactus and Succulent Society of America
